issues.legal_issue: Concurrent findings of bona fide personal requirement do not prevent special-leave review when the appellant establishes that the decisions are manifestly unjust.
material_facts: Three courts had accepted the landlord’s claim that the premises were required bona fide for personal use.

The appellant challenged the concurrent decisions and demonstrated that the lower courts had relied on an unsupported inference, confused need with desire, and failed to consider a material later development.
issues.conclusion: The concurrence of the lower courts was relevant but did not bar review; once the appellant discharged the burden of showing manifest injustice, the Supreme Court had a duty to remedy it.
issues.legal_principle: The jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution is exercised sparingly, and an appellant bears the burden of showing that concurrent decisions are manifestly unjust. Concurrence is not conclusive: when that burden is discharged, the Court may and must remedy the injustice.

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal seeking special leave to challenge a court decision.
predicates.concurrent_lower_court_findings: Two or more lower courts reached the same finding on the issue.
predicates.appellant_shows_manifest_injustice: The appellant demonstrates that the concurrent decision is manifestly unjust.

issues.definition: When a special-leave appeal challenges concurrent lower-court findings and the appellant demonstrates manifest injustice, the Supreme Court reviews and corrects the decision.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord’s personal requirement for eviction must continue to exist when the proceeding is finally decided, and relevant subsequent events must be considered in determining whether relief remains justified.
material_facts: During the proceedings, eviction orders against other tenants became final.
Those orders gave the landlord possession of several other premises in the same building.
The Supreme Court found that possession of those premises more than adequately met the landlord’s asserted requirement, while the appellant’s premises remained occupied.
issues.conclusion: The Court considered the subsequent events and held that there was no justification for evicting the appellant; the eviction petition against the appellant was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: In a tenant-eviction proceeding based on personal requirement, the requirement must continue to exist when the proceeding is finally disposed of, unless the governing statute provides otherwise. A court must evaluate subsequent events that may defeat the claimed need and mould relief accordingly. The Court relied on Hasmat Rai v. Raghunath Prasad, [1981] 3 SCR 605.

predicates.personal_requirement_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks a tenant’s eviction on the ground that the landlord personally requires the premises.
predicates.subsequent_events_provide_other_premises: Events during the proceeding give the landlord possession of other premises.
predicates.other_premises_adequately_meet_claimed_n: The other premises are sufficient to meet the landlord’s asserted personal requirement.

issues.definition: In a personal-requirement eviction proceeding, if later events provide other premises that sufficiently meet the claimed need, the eviction claim is dismissed.

issues.legal_issue: A finding of bona fide personal requirement cannot rest on an unsupported claim of business losses or on the mere fact that the landlord conducts business from rented premises.
material_facts: The landlord claimed that his wholesale business was losing money and that he therefore wished to start a retail business in the premises occupied by the tenants.
The tenant called for the business’s balance sheet, tax returns, and account books, but the landlord did not produce them and said the balance sheet was with an auditor who was away.
The trial court accepted the landlord’s assertion of losses without drawing an adverse inference from the non-production of the documents.

The appellate court treated the fact that the landlord conducted business in rented premises as sufficient to establish bona fide requirement, although that was not the landlord’s stated basis for seeking possession.
issues.conclusion: The lower courts’ assessment of bona fide requirement was flawed: the claimed losses were accepted without the available material evidence, and the appellate court confused need with desire by relying on the fact that the business was conducted in rented premises.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 10(3)(i) and 10(3)(iii) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, the landlord’s asserted personal requirement must be assessed on the evidence and cannot be inferred merely from a desire to occupy premises or from the fact that the landlord’s business is conducted in rented premises. The judgment identifies no earlier case as authority for this evidentiary point.

predicates.personal_requirement_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction on the ground of the landlord’s personal requirement.
predicates.landlord_claims_business_losses: The landlord relies on claimed losses in an existing business to explain the asserted need for the premises.
predicates.material_business_records_are_not_produc: The landlord does not produce available records that would substantiate the claimed business losses after their production is sought.
predicates.need_is_inferred_from_rented_business_pr: A court infers personal need from the fact that the landlord conducts business in rented premises, rather than assessing the landlord’s stated case on evidence.

issues.definition: When a personal-requirement eviction finding rests on an unsubstantiated business-loss claim and an inference from the landlord’s use of rented business premises, the finding is unreliable.

issues.legal_issue: A court considering eviction must take account of the foreseeable consequences of its proposed order and all relevant aspects of the matter.
material_facts: The proposed eviction would displace a tenant from occupied premises.
The appellate court had dismissed the tenant’s concern about being left without premises as immaterial.
The Supreme Court said that courts, including rent tribunals, must consider the foreseeable consequences of an eviction order.
issues.conclusion: The tenant’s likely displacement could not properly be treated as a matter of no moment; the court had to consider the foreseeable consequences of the order along with the other aspects of the case.
issues.legal_principle: Whether or not the governing law specifically requires it, a court must have regard to all relevant aspects of the matter and the foreseeable consequences of the order it proposes to make.

predicates.court_is_considering_tenant_eviction: The court is deciding whether to order a tenant’s eviction.
predicates.proposed_order_would_displace_tenant: The proposed eviction order would displace the tenant from occupied premises.

issues.definition: When a court considers eviction that would displace a tenant, it considers the foreseeable consequences of that order.
